Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
Michael was fifty years old, a clinical psychologist with a thriving private practice, when a colleague raped him in his own office after a late supervision meeting. The man’s breath carried the sharp, sweet smell of whiskey—Michael had noticed it earlier and felt a flicker of unease, but he had dismissed it. The assault itself was swift and wordless. Michael remembered the pressure of the other man’s body, the sickness rising in his throat, the way his own limbs had turned to something not his own. He did not fight. He did not scream. Later, as he lay on the floor, he heard sirens—an ambulance passing somewhere outside—and the sound seemed to pin him there, as if the world were rushing toward a disaster that had already happened inside him. He never reported it. He told no one. He simply got up, drove home in silence, and slept next to his wife without waking her.

In the weeks that followed, Michael noticed that certain moments seemed to steal his breath. A patient’s cologne, if it had an alcohol base, would send a wave of nausea through him. He would be sitting in a session, listening to someone talk about their week, when suddenly his chest would tighten and his mind would go blank—not an image, not a word, just the full raw terror of that night, as though his body were reliving something his brain refused to show him. He could not describe what had happened to him. When his wife asked why he seemed distant, he said only that work had been stressful. Part of him believed that if he ever tried to put it into words, the words would fall apart, or worse, that speaking it would make it real in a way he could not survive.

He found himself pushing the memory away before it could fully arrive, like slamming a door on something crawling toward him. He knew there was more—details, a sequence, a beginning—but he never let himself reach the end. All he knew was that he felt hollowed out. He had always defined himself by his capacity to listen, to hold others’ suffering without flinching. Now he felt dead inside, as if his own emotional life had been siphoned out of him. He began to question whether he was still capable of being a psychologist at all. How could he sit with a trauma survivor when he could not even face his own? He started avoiding new trauma referrals, claiming a full schedule. He moved his office to a different floor because the hallway near the old room smelled faintly of antiseptic and stale coffee—reminders he could not stand.

His marriage suffered. His wife complained that he was “not there,” and he had no answer because she was right. What frightened Michael most was the growing conviction that he had become an object—not a person, just a thing that had been used. He would catch his reflection and not recognize himself; he felt like a stranger wearing his own skin. The faintest hint of discomfort in his body—a tight shirt, a closed space—would trigger a panicked alertness, as though danger were hiding in the ordinary.

After six months of this, his wife gave him an ultimatum. He sought out a trauma specialist, a colleague he trusted but had been avoiding. In her office, he sat rigidly, unable to explain why he was there. What he wanted, more than anything, was to feel like a person again. What he feared was that to get there, he would have to remember everything—and that once he did, he might not survive what he found.
